name: Carob (Ceratonia siliqua)
short: Case: man died of liver failure, severe low blood sugar after excess carob. Allergy titles: pod, gum. Bean juice, 80 children randomised: no metabolic problem; concentrate, 52 adults: no side effects.
text: This entry covers carob taken by mouth (carob pod powder, carob bean juice, a carob fruit concentrate, and carob in a case report and in supplement trials whose abstracts do not give the form); data on carob gum, carob bean flour, carob seed flour and locust bean gum are labelled separately, because they are different products. Serious harm (case report, by mouth; the abstract does not say which carob product was eaten or how much): a 34-year-old man with obsessive-compulsive disorder was admitted with fever, altered consciousness and jaundice, with severe low blood sugar, liver failure and a critically low prothrombin level; his condition was attributed to excessive consumption of carob, which he believed helped digestion, and carob poisoning was suspected because no other cause was found. He died of acute liver failure despite intensive treatment. In a 90-day randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a carob fruit liquid concentrate in 52 adults with prediabetes, the product was well tolerated and no adverse effects were recorded. In a randomised trial in 80 children aged 4 to 48 months in hospital with acute diarrhoea, carob bean juice added to oral rehydration solution did not lead to any clinical metabolic problem; high blood sodium occurred in three children given the solution alone and in none given it with carob bean juice, and three children were excluded for excessive vomiting (the abstract does not say from which group). In a randomised placebo-controlled trial in 41 infants aged 3 to 21 months with acute diarrhoea, tannin-rich carob pod powder was described as well accepted and tolerated, without listing events. The abstracts of a 2024 meta-analysis of four randomised trials of carob supplements in 236 infertile men, and of a 12-week randomised trial with carob, ginseng and placebo groups of 30 infertile men each, give no adverse-event data and do not describe the carob product beyond calling it a supplement. Allergy: in a double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge study in 12 children with peanut anaphylaxis, skin tests were positive to carob pulp in 3 and to raw carob bean in 6, but none reacted when given raw or cooked carob to eat. A case report on carob pods (the form in the infant pod-powder trial) is titled 'Immediate hypersensitivity to carob pods'; the record has no abstract, so nothing more, including the route, can be reported. Other carob products (gum and flour, not the products tested in the trials above): case reports are titled 'Allergy to carob gum in an infant', 'FPIES induced by locust bean gum in an infant' (a delayed food-protein reaction of the gut), 'Urticaria and angioedema due to ingestion of carob gum', and rhinitis and asthma from occupational exposure to carob bean flour; these records have no abstract, so nothing more can be reported. A 2017 scientific opinion of the European Food Safety Authority states that locust bean gum is made from the ground seed endosperm of the carob tree; it found no safety concern for the general population at its reported uses as a food additive, but says the available data do not allow an adequate safety assessment of the gum in foods for special medical purposes for infants and young children, who may be more susceptible to its gut effects because of their underlying condition. A further record, with no abstract, is titled 'Infant formulas thickened with carob bean gum causing false-positive galactomannan test reactivity' (a blood test used to detect fungal infection). Interactions: in a study in six healthy volunteers, carob seed flour added to a formula diet taken with digoxin (a heart medicine) gave significantly higher blood digoxin concentrations than the diet alone; this concerns seed flour, not pod products. In a case report, an infant girl taking levothyroxine for congenital hypothyroidism had worsening thyroid tests after starting a formula thickened with carob bean gum for reflux; the tests improved within 14 days of stopping the formula, and the authors suggest the formula may affect levothyroxine absorption. This concerns carob bean gum in formula, not carob pod products.
